newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SIGHTING OF VENUS LIFTS GLOOM AT RAINY WIMBLEDON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SIGHTING OF VENUS LIFTS GLOOM AT RAINY WIMBLEDON.

text.p: The news that Venus had been sighted caused a stampede on a wet day at Wimbledon on Friday.
Thick rainclouds obscured any view of the planets and it was the earthly Venus who attracted all the attention.

Venus Williams is a star in her own right already. For a young woman who has yet to win a professional tournament and who lasted just two rounds in her only previous Grand Slam event, she exudes the confidence and charisma of a seasoned champion.
"I guess I'm something a bit different," smiled the 17-year-old American as she surveyed a packed media interview room.

The hundreds of hair beads in Wimbledon's purple and green colours, the height -- she is 1.86 metres and still growing -- and the eye-catching silver dress she wore at the French Open have already singled out Williams as something different.
Add to that the teasing hype about her playing ability and the self-confidence oozing from every pore and Williams is a gift to women's tennis.

Journalists frustrated by three days of rain delays were delighted when Williams, who has been hanging around all week waiting to play her first-round match, agreed to give a news conference on Friday.
As the rush for seats subsided Williams, accompanied by younger sister Serena, folded herself into a chair, shook her beads and waited.
Britain's tabloid press wanted to know if she had a boyfriend. An American reporter asked what shampoo she used. Williams took it all in her stride.
"I do enjoy all the attention," she admitted. Did she deserve it, a fearless questioner asked. Williams did not flinch. "Obviously I think right now I'm playing some pretty good tennis," she smiled.
"Do you admire any other players?" someone else asked.
Williams was blunt. "No, I don't. I think a lot of players are doing well and playing good but I don't actually look up to them. I don't see why I would do that.
"I don't think you can actually play on a tour...and say: 'Oh no, I'm not my favourite player, someone else is my favourite player'," she said.
The Williams sisters, who hope to start playing doubles together on the tour later this year, have been carefully held back from too much exposure to tennis by their father and coach Richard.
Mindful of such burnout victims as Jennifer Capriati and Andrea Jaeger, Mr Williams has kept Serena, 15, off the junior tour and limited Venus's appearances as a professional.
She has played in just five tournaments this year, with her best performance being at Indian Wells where she reached the quarter-finals.
In the French Open she lost in the second round to Nathalie Tauziat who beat her again at the same stage in Eastbourne, Williams's first tournament on grass.
At Wimbledon she is due to meet Polish teenager Magdalena Grzybowska in the first round -- if the rain ever stops long enough for her to get on court.
Williams, a Jehovah's Witness, is calm about the constant rain delays which have spoiled her first visit to Wimbledon.

"I am not frustrated at all, I think maybe a lot of players are but I am just fine," said Williams who has been visiting the Tower of London with her mother and sister, playing video games and even answering the telephones in the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) office.

Williams's only worry is what will happen if some of the beads fly off her braids while she is playing. She has been warned by the WTA that umpires will call a let if it happens once or twice but might then deduct a point if it happened again and they felt her opponent had been distracted.
But Williams dismissed the issue. "No opponent is going to be looking at my hair," she said. "If they were looking at my hair they wouldn't be interested in playing tennis."
